interviewQuestions.question: When would you denormalize this data model?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd denormalize only once I've confirmed two things: reads vastly outnumber writes for this data, and the join cost is measurably too high for a real, frequent query — not on a general belief that joins are inherently slow. If a comment feed renders constantly and a commenter's display name barely ever changes, I'd embed the name directly on the comment to skip the join on every read.

I'd say out loud what I'm accepting in exchange: the embedded name can go stale the moment the source user record changes, since it was copied at write time. I'd either build an explicit propagation path to update every copy on a rename, or accept the staleness if it's tolerable for this product.

I'd also mention that I'd measure the join's actual cost before committing — a join adding a couple of milliseconds isn't worth this trade, one turning a fast lookup into a slow one under real load might be.

**Testing:** whether you tie denormalization to a measured need and accept its cost explicitly, instead of applying it reflexively.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Deciding when to denormalize

interviewQuestions.question: The user's name needs to update everywhere within a day — how do you propagate that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd emit an event on rename and have a background job or event consumer update every embedded copy — all of that user's comments, in this example — asynchronously rather than synchronously in the request path. A one-day window is generous enough that this can run as a batched or rate-limited job instead of an urgent real-time update, which keeps the write cost manageable.

I'd flag the scale consideration honestly: for a user with an unusually large number of comments, this could still mean touching millions of rows for a single rename. That's worth surfacing as a reason some systems deliberately cap how aggressively they embed data that's genuinely likely to change, or fall back to a reference instead of an embed for exactly this kind of relationship.

I'd also make sure the propagation job is idempotent and safely re-runnable, since a rename event getting redelivered shouldn't cause any corruption.

**Testing:** whether you can design a concrete, scale-aware propagation mechanism instead of hand-waving 'we'd sync it.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Propagating a rename within a day

interviewQuestions.question: Would a cache achieve the same win without denormalizing the data model itself?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Often, yes, and I'd name it as a real alternative rather than jumping straight to denormalizing. A read-through cache in front of the join can absorb most of the read cost without ever duplicating data into the primary model, and invalidating one cache entry on a user update is arguably simpler than hunting down and updating every denormalized copy scattered across other records.

The honest trade-off between the two options: caching adds an additional system to operate and still carries a staleness window until the cache entry expires or is explicitly invalidated, while denormalizing avoids running an extra system but bakes the staleness risk permanently into the data model itself.

I'd lean toward caching first when the access pattern doesn't demand a change to the model, and reserve denormalization for cases where the read pattern is fundamental enough that I want it reflected in the data shape itself.

**Testing:** whether you consider caching as a genuine alternative instead of treating denormalization as the only lever for read speed.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Caching as an alternative
